content.theory:
`std::string` (from `<string>`) is the modern way to handle text in C++.

Common operations:

```cpp
#include <string>

std::string text = "Hello, World";

text.length()          // 12
text.size()            // 12 (same thing)
text[0]                // 'H' — access a character
text.append("!")       // adds to the end
text += "!";           // same, simpler
text.substr(0, 5);     // "Hello"
text.find("World");    // 7 (position, or std::string::npos if not found)
```

Some functions return a **new** string while others modify in place — `append` and `+=` modify, `substr` returns a copy.

String vs char array: C++ also has `char` arrays (C-style strings), but `std::string` handles length and memory for you — always prefer it.

Turn a string into a number with `std::stoi`:

```cpp
int n = std::stoi("42");
```

Check the size with `.size()` and remember it counts characters:

```cpp
std::string name = "Ada";
std::cout << name.size();  // 3
```
